reviewStatus: Drafted from verified sources; pending independent clinician review before clinical release.
commonErrors: Classifying before neurophysiology can distinguish conduction block from axonal loss.
name: Seddon Classification of Nerve Injury

version.label: Seddon (1943): neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis
version.detail: Three classes by the structures injured. Sunderland's five degrees subdivide these.

purpose: Classifies peripheral nerve injury by the structures disrupted.

options.label: Neurapraxia: Focal conduction block with intact axons (myelin injury)
Axonotmesis: Axonal disruption with preserved connective tissue sheaths; Wallerian degeneration
Neurotmesis: Complete disruption of the nerve including its connective tissue

resultStates.label: Neurapraxia
resultStates.summary: Focal conduction block with intact axons (myelin injury).
resultStates.detail: Recovery usually complete within weeks to months.

resultStates.label: Axonotmesis
resultStates.summary: Axonal disruption with preserved connective tissue sheaths; Wallerian degeneration.
resultStates.detail: Recovery by regeneration (about 1 mm/day), often good.

resultStates.label: Neurotmesis
resultStates.summary: Complete disruption of the nerve including its connective tissue.

clinicalContext.text: Determines expected recovery and whether surgical repair may be needed.

clinicalInsights.text: The class is often clear only with time and serial neurophysiology; early injuries can be mixed.

limitations.text: Often cannot be determined at presentation; mixed injuries are common.

limitations: Does not separate the degrees within axonotmesis that differ in recovery (see Sunderland).

confounders.effect: Wallerian degeneration takes days to show.

guideSections.howToPerform: Combine mechanism, examination, serial neurophysiology and operative findings.
guideSections.clinicalContext: Guides expectations and timing of surgery.

sources.citation: Seddon HJ. Three types of nerve injury. Brain. 1943;66(4):237-288.
